stories.headline: OCTOBER CPI RUNS HOT AGAIN AS CORE PRICES RISE 0.3% FOR A SECOND STRAIGHT MONTH
stories.body: Headline CPI rose 0.4% month-over-month in October, hotter than expected, while core CPI (ex-food and energy) rose 0.3% for the second consecutive month, a pace economists flagged as crossing Fed Governor Waller's own threshold for weighing a bigger hike. Because last year's 43-day government shutdown left the BLS without usable October 2025 price data, the agency could not publish an official year-over-year rate, so markets are trading off the monthly run-rate alone.
stories.explain: A 0.3% monthly core print annualizes to roughly 3.6-4%, well above the Fed's 2% target, and two months in a row of that pace is what shifts a 'data-dependent' Fed from holding to actively debating hike size rather than just hike probability. The missing year-over-year comparison matters because it strips away the number headline writers and some trading algorithms default to, forcing everyone, including the FOMC, to lean more heavily on the monthly and three-month annualized trend, which is exactly the number that came in hot today.

stories.headline: STOCKS SLIDE AS HOT INFLATION DATA ERASES PART OF MONDAY'S RALLY
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.37% to 7,521, the Dow dropped roughly 0.3% to about 52,232, and the Nasdaq fell 0.59%, giving back a chunk of Monday's sharp bounce as the CPI print cemented higher December rate-hike odds. Tech led the retreat, with the AI-infrastructure names that rallied hardest a day earlier among the worst performers.
stories.explain: Monday's rally was built partly on falling volatility and short-covering after last week's selloff, a move that is mechanically fragile because it depends on the macro backdrop staying calm; today's hot CPI reintroduces exactly the kind of rate-path uncertainty that rally was pricing away. Growth and AI-infrastructure stocks are the most rate-sensitive because more of their valuation sits in cash flows far in the future, so a higher discount rate from firmer hike odds compresses their present value more than it does for value or defensive names.

stories.headline: NVIDIA EXTENDS SLIDE AS BOARD'S FOREIGN-INTELLIGENCE PROBE INTO HUANG CONTINUES
stories.body: Nvidia shares fell further Tuesday, compounding last week's drop, as the independent board committee's investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's ties to a Chinese tech executive suspected of espionage remains open with no set timeline. The stock's weakness is adding to, not just following, today's broader tech selloff tied to the CPI print.
stories.explain: With two distinct negative catalysts now stacked on the same stock, idiosyncratic key-person/governance risk from the Huang probe and systematic rate risk from the hot CPI, options markets price them as compounding rather than offsetting, which is why Nvidia is underperforming peers that only face the rate-driven selloff. Because Nvidia carries one of the largest single-stock weights in both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, its decline is also mechanically dragging down the index-level numbers reported above by more than its market-cap share would suggest for a typical constituent.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS FIRM FURTHER UNDER CHAIR WARSH AFTER HOT CPI
stories.body: Fed funds futures continue to price a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting as the most likely outcome, with odds that were already near 85% after the Fed's late-October decision firming further on today's data. Chair Kevin Warsh's inflation-focused framework has kept the bar for a December hold high given back-to-back hot core prints.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures imply hike probability by pricing the expected average overnight rate over the contract period against the current rate, so a shift toward pricing a hike as near-certain reflects the market concluding that two consecutive 0.3% core months leaves the FOMC little room to justify standing pat without looking behind the inflation curve. That near-certainty itself becomes self-fulfilling to a degree: a Fed chair who has built credibility on responding to exactly this kind of data would face a larger communication cost from NOT hiking than from hiking, which is why odds tend to firm rather than reverse once they cross roughly 80%.

stories.headline: YIELDS JUMP, DOLLAR FIRMS AND GOLD SLIDES AS HOT CPI REPRICES RATE PATH
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 12 basis points toward 4.98% and the DXY dollar index gained 0.59% to 102.24 as the hot CPI print pulled forward rate-hike expectations, while gold fell 2.05% to roughly $4,040 an ounce. WTI crude ticked up 0.90% to about $86 a barrel, a relatively muted move against the broader rates repricing.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so when real rates rise, the opportunity cost of holding it rises too, which is the direct mechanical link between today's higher Treasury yields and gold's 2% drop; a stronger dollar amplifies that by making gold costlier for non-dollar buyers. Oil's small gain despite the same hawkish repricing suggests today's move is being read by crude traders as a demand-neutral inflation surprise rather than a fresh growth scare, leaving supply-side OPEC+ oversupply concerns as the bigger swing factor for WTI right now than the rates story.

watchlist: Fed's Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting — hike odds, already near 85% after October's decision, firmed further on today's hot CPI under Chair Kevin Warsh
October PPI (producer prices), due later this week — will test whether CPI's hot core reading is confirmed further upstream in the supply chain
Nvidia board's investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's foreign-intelligence ties — still open with no set timeline; a material finding could reset AI-trade sentiment given Nvidia's index weight
10-year Treasury yield near 4.98% — a push toward 5% would tighten financial conditions meaningfully heading into December
Retail sales and University of Michigan consumer sentiment — next reads on whether households are absorbing higher goods, rent, and energy costs

deepDive.title: When CPI's Year-Over-Year Math Breaks: The Shutdown Hole in the Inflation Data
content: Today's CPI report moved markets on a single, solid number: core prices rose 0.3% month-over-month for the second straight month, enough to firm up December rate-hike odds and pull stocks off Monday's rally. But buried in the release is a stranger fact that didn't make most headlines: the Bureau of Labor Statistics could not publish an official year-over-year inflation rate for October at all. For a finance student used to seeing 'CPI rose X% year-over-year' as the default headline number, that gap is worth understanding, because it is not a one-off quirk; it is a direct, mechanical consequence of last year's 43-day government shutdown, and it tells you something real about how much weight to put on any inflation number right now.

Year-over-year CPI is arithmetically simple: take this month's price index level, divide by the index level from the same month a year earlier, subtract one. The entire calculation depends on having a real, collected index value for the base month. Last year's shutdown ran from early October through mid-November 2025, and the BLS simply never sent survey takers out to collect most October 2025 prices; some data collection is physically done by people visiting stores and checking listed prices, and a lapse in appropriations stops that work outright. There is no revised historical substitute, because the prices were never observed. So when the BLS tried to compute October 2026 versus October 2025, the denominator doesn't exist in any reliable form.

What most people miss is that this doesn't just create a footnote, it creates competing, non-official estimates that can disagree by a full percentage point or more while everyone agrees on the actual monthly data. Axios interpolated the missing October 2025 base by splitting the difference between September and November 2025 prices, arriving at roughly 4.0% headline and 2.8% core year-over-year. The Cleveland Fed's nowcasting model, which uses higher-frequency inputs like gasoline and shelter data to build its own estimate, put core at just 2.48%, half a point lower. Neither is 'the' number; both are informed guesses patched over a hole in the historical record, a situation with no modern precedent, since even the 2013 shutdown only delayed data releases rather than permanently erasing a base period.

The practical takeaway for interpreting today's brief, and the Fed's Dec. 8-9 decision, is that policymakers and traders are being forced to do exactly what the Fed has always claimed to prefer in theory: focus on the monthly and three-month annualized run-rate rather than a backward-looking annual number. That is precisely why today's 0.3% core reading, crossing the threshold officials like Governor Waller have cited for considering a larger move, carried so much weight in moving rate-hike odds and yields, even without a trustworthy year-over-year figure to anchor the headline. Going into December, expect Fed communications and market pricing to keep leaning on monthly core prints and 'supercore' services measures rather than the annual rate, until enough months pass for a clean twelve-month comparison to exist again in late 2026.
